topic: Power: Monarchy & Democracy in Britain c1000 to 2014
subject: history

items.title: Henry VII was a 'modern' monarch — by destroying the nobility
items.claim: How did Henry VII (r. 1485-1509) consolidate power?

options.text: By distributing land widely among loyal nobles
By using bonds and recognisances to financially bind nobles, the Star Chamber to bypass juries, and avoiding war to keep crown finances strong
By creating a standing army of 50,000 men
By moving the capital from London to York

items.reveal:
Henry VII forced nobles to enter bonds — written debts payable to the crown on bad behaviour. By 1509 around two-thirds of the peerage was under bond. Empson and Dudley managed crown revenue ruthlessly.

The Star Chamber, sitting at Westminster, dealt with cases the common-law courts could not — overmighty nobles intimidating juries. Henry VII left £1.5 million in the treasury (his son spent it in a decade). He fought one continental war.
items.why: Henry VII is the boring Tudor — but his fiscal-administrative state is what makes Henry VIII's ambition possible. Modern bureaucratic monarchy starts here, not at the Reformation.

items.title: Elizabeth I's wardrobe was a political instrument
items.claim: How extensive was Elizabeth I's wardrobe at her death?

options.text: A modest collection of state robes

Inventories at her death (1603) recorded around 2,000 gowns, gifts and ceremonial robes; she owned around 80 wigs after smallpox scarring in 1562 and used ceruse make-up to maintain the 'Mask of Youth' image

items.reveal:
Elizabeth survived smallpox in October 1562 with scarring on her face and neck. Ceruse (white lead and vinegar) gave the white complexion seen in portraits — slowly toxic with long-term use.

Nicholas Hilliard's 'Treatise Concerning the Arte of Limning' (1598-1602) reports that painters were instructed not to show shadow on the queen's face after about 1590 — the 'Mask of Youth' image preserved her as eternally young.

The wardrobe was renewed by gifts from courtiers, who chose colours, materials and embroidered devices loaded with political meaning. Roy Strong's 'Gloriana' (1987) catalogued the visual programme.
items.why: Elizabethan court politics was conducted partly through clothes. The 'Virgin Queen' image was constructed by carefully managed wardrobe, portraiture and pageant — a sustained branding exercise of the monarchy.

items.title: Magna Carta was annulled within ten weeks
items.claim: King John sealed Magna Carta at Runnymede on 15 June 1215. What happened next?

options.text: It immediately became the basis of English liberty and was respected by the crown
John wrote to Pope Innocent III, who annulled it as 'shameful and demeaning' on 24 August 1215 — civil war resumed
John was forced to confirm it in Parliament the following year
It was burned by the barons after John refused to enforce it

items.reveal:
Pope Innocent III's bull of 24 August 1215 declared Magna Carta 'null and void of all validity forever', calling it extorted by force. The First Barons' War followed; the barons invited Prince Louis of France to take the throne.

John died of dysentery in October 1216. The charter was reissued by the regents of his nine-year-old son Henry III to win support — that is the version that took root. The 1297 reissue under Edward I is the one on the statute roll.
items.why: Magna Carta as 'the foundation of liberty' is a 17th-century invention (Coke). In 1215 it was a peace treaty between a desperate king and rebellious barons — and it failed within weeks.
